title: Creede Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Creede wells have a 99-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $12,400-$21,900.
h1: Creede, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Creede means looking closely at the local well record, not just assuming mountain water is dependable. Permits within five miles show relatively shallow wells overall, solid reported yields, and a strong connection to fractured bedrock.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records for Creede and nearby areas in Mineral County. It also covers drilling cost, water-level information, environmental concerns, and the questions to ask before buying or building.

sections.heading: What well depth looks like around Creede
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Creede is 99 feet deep. The middle half runs from 67 to 120 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site may be working in that range rather than automatically planning a very deep mountain hole. Half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 43% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

Depth still varies sharply. The 90th-percentile depth is 217 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 1,000 feet. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with granite and gneiss making production dependent on the fractures encountered. A nearby well in the City of Creede, Gerrard, or another local area can help, but it does not guarantee the same result on your lot.

sections.heading: Expected well yield in the Creede area
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The reported distribution is encouraging for household use: 55% produce more than 15 gallons per minute, and 42% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Only 2% are in the 1-to-5-gallon-per-minute range, and none are reported below 1 gallon per minute.

These figures describe reported well tests, not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Yield can be seasonal and a pump test is not the same as unlimited storage. An exempt household-use well still has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Confirm the permit's allowed use, production test, and any augmentation requirement before planning irrigation or additional uses.

sections.heading: Water levels and the local trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 42 feet below the surface. The middle half ranges from 10 to 70 feet, which gives a useful planning range for pump setting, trenching, and water-system design. A shallow static level does not mean the well will produce strongly; storage, fractures, casing, and the completed interval still matter.

The decade figures show a median static level of 36 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 40 feet in the 2020s. That is a modest shift deeper in the available record, but only 79 wells report static water levels, so it is not enough by itself to establish a broad decline across Creede. Ask for the actual measurement date and conditions for any property you are evaluating.

sections.heading: Creede permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
Permit activity has continued over many decades. The records show 7 permits in the 1950s, 4 in the 1960s, 142 in the 1970s, 94 in the 1980s, 165 in the 1990s, 175 in the 2000s, 90 in the 2010s, and 84 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026. That history gives Creede a substantial local record for comparing nearby construction and performance.

The most frequently listed drillers are Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.) with 116 records, Irrigation Engineering & Supp. (Burk, Coy) with 109, and Larry Burk Drilling (Burk, Larry) with 80. Older permits may not reflect current pricing or equipment, but they can reveal depth, aquifer description, casing, and test results near a parcel.

sections.heading: What a new well costs near Creede
sections.html:
Creede's fractured mountain bedrock—granite and gneiss—makes the drilling bid sensitive to footage, access, casing, grout, and the amount of work needed to complete the hole. The local drilling rate model is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 99-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone works out to about $6,400 to $9,900.

A finished system is more than the borehole. Including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled total at the median depth is about $12,400 to $21,900. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed quote. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing, low yield, or a long utility run can change the bid substantially.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building on a lot
sections.html:
The main water risks are not limited to depth. Fractured-bedrock wells can encounter an unproductive zone or a dry hole even when nearby properties do well. Review the well construction report, pump test, static level, casing and grout details, and the permit's approved use. Water testing is also important: mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 447 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites.

Mining history makes location-specific testing especially sensible. Check well water for health-related contaminants with a qualified laboratory, and keep the well separated from septic components as required by the applicable rules. Confirm the building site has room for the well, septic system, access, and utility trenching before closing or starting excavation.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Creede
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a countywide average. Pull the DWR permit, construction report, recorded use, yield test, and static water level. Then compare nearby wells in the City of Creede and the surrounding mountain communities, while recognizing that fractured rock can change over short distances. A driller can use those records to prepare a more defensible depth and access estimate.

For a vacant lot, verify legal water supply, septic suitability, driveway access, electrical routing, and any augmentation-plan issue before purchase. Most permits in this area are domestic or household use at 86%, while 8% are monitoring, 4% stock, and 1% irrigation. If your plans include irrigation or uses beyond the permit, resolve that water-rights question early.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Creede, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well within five miles of Creede is 99 feet deep. The middle half runs from 67 to 120 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 217 feet. Half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, but the deepest record reaches 1,000 feet, so local records should guide any site-specific bid.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Creede?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate for Creede's fractured mountain bedrock is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 99-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $6,400 to $9,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $12,400 to $21,900. Difficult access or a deeper hole can raise the quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Creede?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 15.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 55% above 15 gallons per minute and 42% between 5 and 15. These are reported tests, not guarantees. Fractured bedrock can produce very differently from one lot to the next.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Creede, Colorado?
faq.a: A permit does not prove that water is safe to drink. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory, especially because the mapped area includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 447 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Review construction details and test results before relying on the water for a home.

faq.q: Are Creede wells getting deeper or running lower?
faq.a: Reported median static water levels were 36 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 40 feet in the 2020s. That suggests a modestly deeper measured level, but only 79 wells report static levels, so it does not establish a regionwide decline. Ask for the specific property's measurement date, level, and well-construction record.
